headline: Bonito Talk Out of the Race Has the Niantic Fleet Watching — Bluefish Are Still Doing the Real Work
subhead: Waterford and Niantic boats are grinding bluefish and sea bass while everyone keeps one eye on the Race for the first bonito to slide in from Block Island.
body_markdown:
Walk into any tackle shop from Niantic to Waterford right now and the conversation starts the same way: has anybody seen a bonito yet? The word out of Block Island and Point Judith is that they've been thick for a couple weeks, and with the Race sitting right at our doorstep, the fleet's been half-expecting one of the drift boats to come back with a story. Nobody's confirmed it in this zone yet — but the water's set up for it. New London's reading around 69.4 degrees, and there's a real gradient running west to east, with Kings Point up near 71. That kind of stair-step is exactly how these fish walk west along the Sound, riding the warmer edge until they find bait to hold on. Keep an ear out over the next several days, because if bonito show up in Twotree Island Channel or off the Race, it'll be the first real sign the push has crossed the state line.

In the meantime, the bread and butter out here is bluefish, and they're not asking anybody's permission. Bunker schools have been thick in Niantic Bay and stacking up around Black Point, and the blues have been all over them — this is the pattern we flagged last week, that bluefish activity was going to track bunker density, and that's exactly what's playing out. Drift boats working bunker schools off McCook Point and along the mouth of the Niantic River have had steady action on diamond jigs and bunker spoons, with some boats doing well on cut bunker chunks fished on wire leader in 15 to 25 feet. These aren't monster blues across the board — there's a mix of 3- to 6-pound fish with some better ones mixed in — but they've been reliable enough that mates are steering people toward them when the rest of the bite gets picky. Topwater guys throwing poppers early in the morning around the bait schools have had some violent strikes, worth doing if you're on the water at first light before the boat traffic pushes the bunker deeper.

Fluke have softened up the way they always do this time of year, and it's fair to call it a mixed bag rather than a hot bite. The warm surface water in the back of Niantic Bay has pushed fish out toward better-oxygenated structure — Hole-in-the-Wall and the channel edges around Twotree have been holding better fish than the flats. Boats working 35 to 45 feet with white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow along the bottom on the last of the ebb, have been picking at keepers in that 18- to 20-inch class, with the occasional 4- or 5-pounder mixed in. This is exactly the transition we called last week — not a collapse, just fluke sliding toward structure and deeper water the way they do every late August. They'll stay catchable into September if you follow them off the flats and onto the drops.

Black sea bass have been the most dependable structure fish on the beat. Black Point reef and the rockpiles off McCook have been giving up decent numbers on squid strips and green crab fished on high-low rigs in 30 to 50 feet, with the better bite coming on the last two hours of the incoming when the current slackens enough to hold bottom without needing a pound of lead. Sizes have been mixed — plenty of shorts to sort through, but enough 14- to 16-inch fish in the mix to make a trip worthwhile if you're patient about moving around the structure.

Striped bass remain the wildcard, and right now they're still in a holding pattern rather than a blitz. There are fish around — some being picked off structure at Hole-in-the-Wall and along the current seams off Black Point on bucktails and swim shads — but the bunker haven't concentrated enough yet to trigger the kind of surface chaos everyone's waiting for. The moon building toward full over the next several days should start changing that. More current means bait gets pushed and squeezed into tighter pockets, and that's usually when the bass stop nibbling around the edges and start committing. If there's one thing worth watching closely heading into Labor Day week, it's whether the bunker schools in Niantic Bay start balling up the way they have in years past when the tide gets some teeth back in it.

For the next few days, the smart play is still bluefish and sea bass while keeping a rod rigged for a quick bucktail cast if stripers show themselves on bait. Wind and boat traffic will both pick up over the holiday weekend, so early starts matter more than usual — get out ahead of the fleet on the last of the ebb, work the bunker schools before they scatter, and don't be shocked if somebody radios in a bonito sighting near the Race before this week is out. The water's right for it. Whether the fish cooperate is the only question left.
